panels.figure_caption: Case 5: baseline anterior, lateral, and posterior views of a 44-year-old male with stage II lipedema (A) Anterior, (B) lateral, and (C) posterior photographs demonstrate bilateral, symmetrical subcutaneous fat accumulation predominating in the thighs and buttocks, with sharp demarcation above the ankles and sparing of the feet. Note the “wide legs” phenotype and relative preservation of lower-leg contour despite overall adipose excess. This patient had post-viral hypothyroidism on levothyroxine and a positive family history (sister), and these images were captured prior to initiation of the ketogenic diet and endocrine follow-up.
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed stage II lipedema with bilateral fat accumulation in the lower extremities and notable capillary fragility (Figure 5). Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan confirmed 38.5% total body fat with disproportionate distribution in the lower limbs. Adjusted BMI calculations and fat ratios supported the lipedema diagnosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histology of dermal vessels from thigh skin of a woman with Stage 1 lipedema. The panel visibly shows the published abnormal vessel phenotype criteria (rounded endothelial cells, perivascular immune cell infiltrate, enlarged perivascular space) and densely packed dermal collagen consistent with fibrotic change. Real human patient tissue with explicit disease attribution in the caption. B: H&E histology of the dermis from thigh skin of a woman with Stage 3 lipedema, with the epidermis base visible at the top. The panel shows an elongated vessel with multiple lumens and wide spacing of collagen fibrils, contrasting with the stage 1 panel. Real human patient tissue with explicit disease attribution; the histologic features are not covered by the allowed vocabulary and are therefore listed as proposed findings.

panels.figure_caption: Dermal vessels from thigh skin of women with lipedema. (A) Lumens of two dermal vessels (*) from a woman with Stage 1 lipedema. Abnormal vessel phenotype: black arrows denote rounded endothelial cells. Dotted arrow points to perivascular immune cell infiltrate. The white arrow denotes the enlarged perivascular space. Note the close packing of the maroon-colored collagen fibers in the dermis with almost no space between. H&E. 60 × . (B) An elongated vessel with multiple lumens (*) in the dermis of a woman with Stage 3 lipedema; the base of the epidermis can be seen at the top of the picture. Note the lack of AVP and the wide spacing of collagen fibrils in the dermis (black arrows). H&E. 40 × to allow clear visualization of spaces. AVP, abnormal vessel phenotype; H&E, hematoxylin and eosin.
in_text_mentions: All vessels in the papillary and reticular dermis of skin samples were scored for abnormal or normal blood vessel phenotype by microscopy at 40 × magnification by two different observers. The number of abnormal vessels over the total number of vessels evaluated was multiplied by 100 to obtain a percent, and then, scores were averaged. A vessel was considered to have an abnormal phenotype if the following published criteria were met: (1) obvious perivascular space as in lymphedema11,12; (2) rounded endothelial cells17,18; and (3) perivascular immune cell infiltrate (Fig. 1).8,19

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: High-frequency breast ultrasound from the lipedema study cohort showing increased echogenicity of the fibrous septa, lobulated adipose architecture, and diffuse stromal thickening—imaging correlates of fibrotic adipose tissue in breast involvement of lipedema. Real human patient image; disease attribution supported by the disease-focused article title (Breast Imaging Findings in Women with Lipedema) together with specific captioned manifestations; not a diagram, control, animal, or other-disease panel. Breast is an uncommon lipedema site, so confidence is moderate. B: Standard mediolateral oblique and craniocaudal mammography views from the same lipedema cohort patient demonstrating diffuse fibroadipose density and a homogeneous non-nodular parenchyma, consistent with fibrotic adipose tissue. Real human patient imaging attributed to lipedema via the disease-focused article title and specific captioned findings; mammographic density...

in_text_mentions: 45% of patients exhibited a predominantly fibro-glandular pattern characterized by a dense fibrous component. Calcifications or microcalcifications—mostly benign and in some cases with dystrophic appearance—were present in 21% of patients. Marked breast asymmetry or tuberous breast morphology was reported in 6%.

The image clearly shows symmetric columnar leg enlargement and feet sparing. The white rectangle is a privacy mask, not an annotation. [raw subtype: type II]

panels.figure_caption: First-degree female cousin of the male patient with a lipedema diagnosis. The patient’s cousin, who shares the same maternal lineage, presents a classic lipedema phenotype with symmetric enlargement of the lower limbs, sparing the feet, and a negative Stemmer sign. Based on clinical evaluation, the case is consistent with type II, stage 2 lipedema, involving buttocks, hips, and thighs with moderate skin surface irregularity. Body Mass Index: 28.4 kg/m2. Waist-to-Height ratio: 0.44.
in_text_mentions: a female cousin. A first-degree cousin, the daughter of his mother’s brother, shared the same phenotype, consented to participate, and underwent clinical evaluation. She exhibited classical lipedema features consistent with established diagnostic criteria (Figure 2). Overall, the clinical findings and family history substantiated the diagnosis of early-stage (I–II) type 2 lipedema, characterized by symmetrical fat accumulation from the hips to the knees with pain and tenderness. Written informed consent for the publication of clinical images was obtained from both the patient and his relative.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Intraoperative photograph shows manual expression of fibrotic lipedema fat nodules from the lower leg, consistent with the captioned advanced-stage lipedema manifestation. B: Intraoperative view shows multiple extracted firm lobulated adipose nodules from lipedema tissue during manual extraction. C: Gross specimen view of evacuated lipedema fat nodules with a ruler, showing the firm lobulated fibrotic adipose tissue characteristic of advanced lipedema.
